profile.goal: detect and hunt threats with Elastic Security: write ES|QL hunting queries, understand and tune detection rules (EQL, KQL, threshold, ES|QL rules) and investigate alerts
profile.background: comfortable with SQL and Linux; new to Elasticsearch

title: Threat Hunting and Detection Engineering with Elastic Security
summary: By the end, the learner will be able to explore security data in Elasticsearch, write and refine ES|QL threat hunts, and choose, create, and tune Elastic Security detection rules using KQL, EQL, threshold logic, and ES|QL. They will also be able to triage an alert, pivot into related events, and check that rules are producing reliable results.

modules.title: Build a mental model of Elastic Security data
modules.summary: Learn the Elasticsearch concepts needed to understand where security events live, how their fields affect queries, and how to confirm data is available before hunting.

lessons.title: Elasticsearch essentials for security analysts
objectives: Explain the difference between an Elasticsearch document, an index, a data stream, and a field mapping.
Identify why a field’s mapped type matters when filtering, grouping, or searching its values.
Describe why timestamped, mostly append-only security events are commonly stored in data streams.

lessons.title: Check your security data in Discover
objectives: Verify that a chosen security data source contains events in the selected time range.
Inspect an event and identify useful fields such as @timestamp, event.category, event.type, host.name, and user.name.
Explain how integrations and ECS field normalization help security rules work across data sources.

modules.title: Hunt with ES|QL
modules.summary: Use Discover and Elastic Security’s investigation workspace to move from a question about activity to filtered, grouped, and contextualized hunt results.

lessons.title: ES|QL query fundamentals in Discover
objectives: Run an ES|QL query using FROM and identify the data source it searches.
Use WHERE, KEEP, SORT, and LIMIT to filter and shape event results.
Use STATS with BY to count events by a security-relevant field, and explain how pipe order affects results.
Contrast ES|QL’s pipe-based processing with the learner’s existing SQL experience.

lessons.title: Turn a threat hypothesis into an ES|QL hunt
objectives: Write and run a query that filters process or authentication events using relevant fields and values.
Use STATS, COUNT_DISTINCT, or time bucketing to assess event volume, spread, or timing.
Refine a hunt by inspecting its returned fields and adjusting the query when results do not support the hypothesis.

lessons.title: Enrich and correlate a hunt in Timeline
objectives: Use LOOKUP JOIN in a hunt to add context from a lookup index.
Build a chronological view of relevant events across multiple data sources.
Open Timeline and use its ES|QL workflow to investigate related security events.

modules.title: Select and write event-based detection rules
modules.summary: Learn how Elastic Security detections turn matching source events into alerts, then practice two different kinds of event logic: a KQL field match and an EQL event sequence.

lessons.title: Detection rules, alerts, and choosing a rule type
objectives: Describe how a detection rule evaluates source events and produces alerts.
Choose between a custom query, EQL, threshold, and ES|QL rule for a set of example detection goals.
Explain why Elastic Security detection rules are distinct from Kibana Universal Alerting rules.
Identify the key schedule, severity, risk score, and alert-volume settings shared by detection rules.

lessons.title: Write a KQL custom query rule
objectives: Write a KQL query using field-value conditions, Boolean operators, and parentheses.
Use a wildcard or field-existence condition in a query, and identify when a leading wildcard may be costly.
Create or preview a custom query rule and verify that its data source and query match the intended event pattern.
Explain why a KQL custom query is suitable for a single-event match but not for aggregation or event ordering.

lessons.title: Detect event sequences with EQL
objectives: Write an EQL sequence with ordered event categories and a shared field that links the events.
Identify the timestamp and event-category fields an EQL rule expects, and explain the purpose of a tiebreaker field.
Choose EQL rather than KQL when the detection depends on event order or a missing event.
Use Timeline’s Correlation tab to inspect EQL sequence results.

modules.title: Detect volume patterns and computed conditions
modules.summary: Build detections for event counts and derived results, learning when a threshold rule is simpler and when an ES|QL detection pipeline is needed.

lessons.title: Build a threshold rule for repeated activity
objectives: Configure a threshold rule that counts matching events and groups them by one or more fields.
Explain how the threshold and group-by fields affect which event groups generate alerts.
Describe how a cardinality constraint can distinguish broad activity, such as many unique destination ports, from repeated events against one value.
Select a threshold rule when the detection depends on an event count rather than a single match or ordered sequence.

lessons.title: Create an ES|QL detection rule
objectives: Create an Elastic Security ES|QL rule from a query that filters, transforms, or aggregates source events.
Explain how query result rows become alerts, including the difference between aggregating and non-aggregating queries.
Describe the role of _id metadata in deduplicating non-aggregating ES|QL rule results and identify the version-specific behavior documented by Elastic.
Choose ES|QL when computed fields or pipeline aggregation are required, rather than using a KQL or EQL rule.

modules.title: Investigate alerts, tune, and verify
modules.summary: Complete the workflow by examining alert context, reducing noise with the appropriate mechanism, and checking that detections run as intended.

lessons.title: Triage an alert and investigate related activity
objectives: Use an alert’s rule description, alert reason, highlighted fields, severity, host, and user to summarize what triggered it.
Pivot from an alert into Timeline and query related events with KQL, EQL, or ES|QL.
Use the process analyzer or Session View, when available for the alert, to examine surrounding process activity.
Record an investigation note or attach relevant work to a case.

lessons.title: Tune detections and monitor rule health
objectives: Choose whether to narrow rule logic, add an exception, suppress repeated alerts, or snooze actions for a given noise scenario.
Apply a tuning change while explaining how it preserves or changes the detection’s coverage.
Preview or manually run a rule against data, then check its execution status and results.
Distinguish a successful execution from a rule that actually generated alerts.
